source_caption:
To fiercely underscore the film’s deeply cynical critique of aggressive corporate consumerism, director David Fincher made a highly meticulous, almost obsessive production choice that spans the entire movie. He deliberately placed a Starbucks coffee cup hidden somewhere in the background of nearly every single frame. Rather than objecting to the association with a wildly destructive anarchist plot, the coffee giant completely leaned into the joke, only drawing the line at letting their actual storefront be destroyed on camera. By quietly littering a fiercely anti-capitalist manifesto with the ultimate symbol of mass-market homogenization, Fincher masterfully proves that the most brilliant cinematic satire doesn’t just attack its targets directly, but relentlessly forces the audience to spot their own everyday complacency.

Fight Club (1999), directed by David Fincher, starring Brad Pitt, Edward Norton, Helena Bonham Carter. A fiercely insomniac, deeply disillusioned office worker desperately searching for meaning forms an incredibly dangerous, wildly unpredictable underground fighting ring with a charismatic soap salesman, accidentally sparking a massive, heavily destructive anarchist movement.

source_details.synopsis: Fight Club is a 1999 American film directed by David Fincher starring Brad Pitt, Edward Norton, and Helena Bonham Carter. It is based on the 1996 novel Fight Club by Chuck Palahniuk. Norton plays the unnamed narrator, who is discontented with his white-collar job. He forms a "fight club" with a soap salesman, Tyler Durden (Pitt) and becomes embroiled with an impoverished but beguiling woman, Marla Singer (Bonham Carter). Palahniuk's novel was optioned by Fox 2000 Pictures producer Laura Ziskin, who hired Uhls to write the film adaptation. Fincher was selected because of his enthusiasm for the story.
